title: How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Kepler — Vinoo Ganesh

primary.label: AI Data Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 36%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The FDE methodology—observation, problem definition, ontology, rapid shipping, product leverage—is broadly applicable across all verticals and is not specific to any single application domain.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The field stories involve enterprise operations scenarios: a dispatch/logistics company, enterprise data quality workflows, and cross-team terminology alignment in large organizations.

summary:
Vinoo Ganesh, CEO & Co-Founder of Kepler (kepler.ai), presents a talk on forward deployed engineering (FDE) as a product strategy, drawing on seven years at Palantir where he designed Project Frontline—a rotation program that trained hundreds of software engineers into forward deployed engineers. His central thesis, attributed to Palantir CTO Shyam, is that FDE is not a role or go-to-market function but an extension of the product team that discovers what to build through fieldwork.

He illustrates this with a costly failure: Palantir built Phoenix, a big data storage system, in isolation around 2013. When it hit real customer data, blank values defaulted to epoch (January 1, 1970), generating 2.3 million key spaces requiring 14TB of RAM—dead on arrival. The lesson: software must be co-built while embedded with the customer.

Two field stories demonstrate the FDE approach. A dispatch company's 47-page requirements document (dashboards, metrics, alerts, BI tool, 3-month estimate) was solved by a single Slack alert built in four hours, after on-site observation revealed the dispatcher simply needed to know if trucks were late. A data quality engineer named Maria opposed CSV-to-Parquet migration for a year; on-site observation revealed she manually downloaded CSVs and double-clicked them to spot-check data quality. An overnight-built Parquet viewer unblocked the migration, dropping pipeline execution from 17 hours to 2.

He introduces the ontology principle: enterprises use different terms for the same entity (customers, clients, billing entities, org IDs), which breaks integrations. FDEs must define the nouns and verbs of the enterprise; when customers adopt the product's language, the FDE becomes the linguistic foundation—locked in. Foundry's ontology layer, an accidental discovery at Palantir, enabled subsequent FDEs to do data integrations and sell product.

The cautionary tale is venue.groovy: a temporary Groovy script for data retention at a ~100,000-person customer that spread everywhere within twelve months and was never productized, creating years of support debt. The lesson: every hack goes into production; ship everything like it will run for 18 months because it probably will. The most important calibration skill is knowing what to discard versus fold into the core product—asking whether you'll get a 2am call in six months, what the trade-offs are, and who you hand it off to. Product leverage is the only thing that wins customers, and FDE is the mechanism for building it.
whyItMatters: The concepts in this talk form a coherent methodology for building products through field deployment. The software engineering concepts describe the process: FDE as product strategy frames the engineer's role; co-building with customers and on-site observation define how to discover what to build; rapid prototyping and the under-a-day rule define when to build immediately; problem definition and ownership define who controls the solution; and production-readiness calibration and technical debt management define how to maintain quality over time. The ontology definition and product leverage concepts describe the strategic outcome: field discoveries become durable platform features that lock in customers through language adoption. The AI concepts extend this methodology to the current landscape: ontology definition becomes the semantic foundation that AI systems reason over, data quality engineering becomes critical for AI pipeline reliability, ground truth platforms represent the application of FDE to AI verifiability, and context engineering is reframed as a data engineering problem. Together, they argue that the gap between AI capabilities and production deployment is fundamentally a product engineering problem—not a model capability problem—and FDE methodology is the bridge that closes it.
temporalContext: This video was published on July 28, 2026, at an AI engineering conference. The speaker's comprehensive FDE blog post was published February 2026, and Kepler was introduced in January 2026. The Palantir experiences described span approximately 2013-2020, the Citadel experience 2021-2023, and the Kepler context is current as of 2026. The talk represents established enterprise software engineering practices from Palantir being applied to the emerging AI product landscape, where the gap between AI model capabilities and production deployment reliability is a central challenge. Research was conducted as of August 22, 2026.
takeaways: FDE is a product strategy, not a role or go-to-market function—it is an extension of the product team that discovers what to build through fieldwork.
Customers describe solutions, not problems; the FDE's job is to define the actual problem and what happens next after the solution exists.
If a problem can be solved in under a day, build and ship it immediately—earn trust through small wins before generalizing.
Whoever defines the problem owns the solution, giving FDEs leverage in early sales and control over subsequent product direction.
Every enterprise has overloaded terms for the same entity; defining the ontology—nouns and verbs—makes the FDE the linguistic foundation, which locks in the customer.
Every hack goes into production; if it solves a problem, it is not temporary. Ship everything like it will run for 18 months because it probably will.
The most important FDE skill is calibrating what to discard versus what to fold into the core product—ask whether you'll get a 2am call in six months.
Physical presence on site is essential—residents get the truth, and the most valuable intel never appears in documentation.

concepts.name: Ontology-Based Semantic Modeling for AI Systems
concepts.explanation: The practice of defining structured entity relationships (nouns and verbs) that AI/ML systems consume for reasoning and operations. The transcript describes ontology definition as an enterprise product practice, but it directly underpins how AI systems understand and operate on business data—mapping real-world entities to computable structures.
concepts.importance: As AI systems are deployed in enterprise environments, the ontology layer becomes the semantic bridge between messy real-world data and structured AI reasoning. Palantir Foundry's ontology is confirmed as a real product feature via official documentation.

concepts.name: Data Quality Engineering for AI/ML Pipelines
concepts.explanation: Ensuring data quality and format compatibility is critical for reliable AI/ML pipeline operation. The Maria/Parquet story illustrates how hidden workflow blockers impede the data infrastructure that AI systems depend on, and how resolving them can yield dramatic pipeline performance improvements (17x speedup).
concepts.importance: AI systems are only as reliable as the data pipelines feeding them. The talk demonstrates that data engineering decisions are constrained by human workflows, a lesson directly applicable to AI data infrastructure.

concepts.name: Ground Truth Platforms for Verifiable AI
concepts.explanation: Kepler (kepler.ai), the speaker's company, is building 'the ground truth platform for AI'—infrastructure that prevents LLMs from generating unreliable numbers by providing verifiable, traceable outputs. This is the modern context in which FDE methodology is being applied.
concepts.importance: Connects the FDE methodology to the current AI challenge of building trustworthy, verifiable AI systems, showing how field-deployed engineering practices transfer to AI product development.

concepts.name: Forward Deployed Engineering for AI Products
concepts.explanation: The application of FDE methodology—on-site observation, rapid shipping, ontology definition, and product leverage—to AI product companies, where the gap between AI model capabilities and real-world production deployment is a primary challenge.
concepts.importance: Reframes AI product development as a field-deployment problem rather than a model-capability problem, suggesting that the bottleneck in AI adoption is engineering methodology, not model performance.

concepts.name: Context Engineering as Data Engineering
concepts.explanation: In FDE practice, context engineering—the structuring of information that AI systems operate on—is fundamentally a data engineering problem of defining ontologies and ensuring data quality, rather than a prompt optimization problem. The ontology layer and data quality practices described in the talk are the substrate upon which AI context engineering depends.
concepts.importance: Positions data engineering and ontology definition as prerequisites for effective AI context engineering, shifting the focus from prompt-level optimization to foundational data infrastructure.

concepts.name: Forward Deployed Engineering as Product Strategy
concepts.explanation: FDE is positioned not as a role or go-to-market function but as an extension of the product team that discovers what to build through fieldwork. The FDE embeds with customers, solves small problems to earn trust, and translates field discoveries into product features.
concepts.importance: This is the central thesis of the talk and reframes a common organizational function (customer-facing engineering) as a product discipline, which has implications for how teams are structured and measured.

concepts.name: Co-building with Customer Embedding
concepts.explanation: Software built in isolation without direct customer input leads to catastrophic failure. The Phoenix system was built in perfect isolation, worked under ideal conditions, and crashed on real data—generating 2.3 million key spaces requiring 14TB of RAM.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates the cost of building without embedded customer context and establishes the rationale for why FDEs must be physically present during development.

concepts.name: Enterprise Ontology Definition
concepts.explanation: Every enterprise uses overloaded terms for the same entity (sales says customers, ops says clients, finance says billing entities, devs say org IDs). FDEs must define the nouns and verbs of the enterprise, creating a linguistic foundation that locks in customers when adopted.
concepts.importance: Ontology definition is a strategic product capability that creates vendor lock-in through language adoption, and it is foundational for data integration and semantic consistency across systems.

concepts.name: Technical Debt from Non-Productized Hacks
concepts.explanation: Temporary scripts that solve real problems inevitably become permanent production systems. venue.groovy was a throwaway data retention hack that spread across a ~100,000-person customer within 12 months, was never productized, and created years of support debt.
concepts.importance: Illustrates the compounding cost of technical debt when field solutions are not folded into the core product, a critical lesson for any engineer shipping customer-facing code.

concepts.name: Production-Readiness Calibration
concepts.explanation: The most important FDE skill is calibrating what to ship into the core product versus what to discard. The 2am phone call test—asking whether you'll get a 2am call about this in six months—helps determine if something should be shipped as production-grade or discarded quickly.
concepts.importance: Provides a practical heuristic for managing the tension between rapid field solutions and long-term product quality, which is essential for engineers operating in customer-embedded contexts.

concepts.name: Problem Definition and Solution Ownership
concepts.explanation: Customers describe solutions, not problems. The FDE's job is to extract the real problem from customer-stated requirements. Whoever defines the problem owns the solution, giving FDEs leverage in early sales and control over subsequent product direction.
concepts.importance: Reframes the engineer's role from implementer to problem owner, which changes how engineering teams engage with sales and product decisions.

concepts.name: Rapid Prototyping and the Under-a-Day Rule
concepts.explanation: If a problem can be solved in under a day of work, build and ship it immediately rather than scoping it further. This earns trust through small wins before generalizing into broader product investment.
concepts.importance: Provides a concrete decision rule for when to build immediately versus when to invest in broader scoping, optimizing for customer trust and momentum.

concepts.name: On-Site Observation for Requirements Discovery
concepts.explanation: Physical presence on site is essential for discovering real user problems. The most valuable intelligence never appears in documentation. Signals include users pulling out phones mid-workflow, switching between tools, or performing manual workarounds invisible in requirements docs.
concepts.importance: Challenges the common practice of remote requirements gathering and establishes observation as a primary engineering methodology for discovering what to build.

concepts.name: Product Leverage Through Field-to-Platform Translation
concepts.explanation: Product leverage—translating one-off field solutions into generalized platform features—is the only thing that wins customers. FDEs serve as the mechanism for building this leverage by discovering what to build through fieldwork and folding it into the core product.
concepts.importance: Defines the ultimate goal of FDE work and connects field-level engineering activity to strategic product outcomes and customer retention.

concepts.name: Data Pipeline Migration and Workflow-Centric Quality
concepts.explanation: Migrating data formats (CSV to Parquet) requires understanding actual user workflows, not just technical specifications. The Parquet viewer story shows how a hidden usability blocker (inability to double-click and inspect) delayed a migration that ultimately reduced pipeline execution from 17 hours to 2 hours.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that data engineering decisions are constrained by human workflows, and that resolving workflow-level blockers can unlock dramatic technical improvements.

sections.title: Introduction: FDE origins at Palantir
sections.summary: Vinoo Ganesh introduces his background: software engineer at Palantir who forward deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan, built Project Frontline (~350 engineers trained), and later built a similar program at Citadel. Now building FDE at Kepler with founding engineer Susanna.

sections.title: Phoenix failure and FDE as product strategy
sections.summary: Palantir built Phoenix, a big data storage system, in isolation around 2013. Real customer data with blank values defaulted to epoch, generating 2.3 million Cassandra key spaces requiring 14TB RAM—dead on arrival. The lesson: the gap was lack of co-building while embedded with the customer. FDE is a product strategy, not a role or go-to-market function.

sections.title: Dispatch company: scoping down to a Slack alert
sections.summary: A dispatch company's 47-page requirements doc requested dashboards, 14 metrics, alerts, and a massive BI tool estimated at three months. After four months of scoping, an on-site visit revealed the dispatcher just needed to know if trucks were late. A Slack alert solved it in 4 hours. Customers describe solutions, not problems.

sections.title: Solve in a day, then own the solution
sections.summary: Three questions to ask before building: what's the core goal, what happens after the solution, and how is the customer solving it today. If a problem is solvable in under a day, just build and ship it. Whoever defines the problem owns the solution, which gives FDEs leverage in early sales by earning trust through small wins.

sections.title: The data quality engineer story
sections.summary: Maria, a data quality engineer, opposed migrating CSV to Parquet for a year. On-site observation revealed she manually downloaded CSVs and double-clicked them for spot-checks—impossible with Parquet. They built a parquet viewer overnight; she approved migration in 2 days, and pipeline execution dropped from 17 hours to 2 hours.

sections.title: Watch what users actually do
sections.summary: Observation principles: any repeated task hints at a missing feature; copying between tools, switching tabs, and pulling out a phone during a workflow are all signals. The most valuable intel is never in documentation—it requires physical presence. Ask users: what's the most annoying part of your morning? Earn the right to define product strategy by solving small repetitive problems first.

sections.title: Own the language: clients vs billing entities
sections.summary: Enterprises use different terms for the same entity: sales says customers, ops says clients, finance says billing entities, devs say org IDs. This ambiguity breaks integrations and creates data quality issues. FDEs must define the nouns and verbs of the enterprise. When users adopt your product, they adopt your language—becoming the linguistic foundation locks you in.

sections.title: The ontology and the linguistic layer
sections.summary: Foundry's ontology was an accidental discovery at Palantir. FDEs must identify overloaded terms, integration points between systems, systems of record, and translation layers. Defining the vocabulary and codifying it in the platform makes the FDE the foundation under which every subsequent solution is built. Foundry's ontology enabled later FDEs to do data integrations and sell product.

sections.title: The Groovy script that became a product
sections.summary: A temporary Groovy script written for data retention at a ~100,000-person customer spread everywhere within 12 months. Vinoo's nickname became venue.groovy; wedding attendees wore shirts with the name. The script was never productized, creating years of support debt. Scripts and hacks can fix problems but don't drive product strategy forward—that's solutions architect work, not FDE work.

sections.title: The most important skill: what to discard
sections.summary: Calibrating what to ship is the most important FDE skill. Ask: will I get a 2am phone call about this in 6 months? What are the trade-offs for the product as a whole? Who do I hand this off to? Am I building something so mission-critical I'll be hated when it breaks? Distinguish between solutions to fold into the core product and solutions to discard quickly.

sections.title: Ship everything like it runs forever
sections.summary: Every hack goes into production. If it solves a problem, it's not temporary—it will live forever. The most dangerous words in engineering are 'this is just temporary.' Ship everything like it will run for 18 months, because it probably will. The product-building lens tells you what goes into the core offering versus what wins customer goodwill.

sections.title: FDE as an extension of product
sections.summary: The right FDEs get badged on site, fly to where customers are, ship fixes before leaving, and own those fixes end to end in the product ecosystem. They translate field problems into nouns and verbs that define the foundation of every subsequent solution. Product leverage is the only thing that wins customers. FDE is an extension of the product function, not go-to-market—especially critical for early-stage companies.

organization.name: Kepler
organization.summary: Kepler (kepler.ai) is an early-stage AI infrastructure company founded in 2025 and headquartered in New York, NY. It builds 'the ground truth platform for AI' — infrastructure that separates AI reasoning (intent, language understanding) from deterministic data retrieval (code that fetches data, runs calculations, and cites sources). The result is AI outputs that are traceable, reproducible, and defensible. The first product, Kepler for Finance, is live and in production for investment banking and financial analysis, with 26M+ SEC filings and 40M+ IR documents indexed. A forthcoming Kepler for Industry product will extend the platform to any domain. The founding team includes senior engineers from Palantir (nearly 50 combined years), Citadel, Meta, and Stanford. The company is backed by founders of OpenAI (Pam Vagata), Meta AI Research (Keith Adams), MotherDuck, dbt Labs, Outerbounds, and Square/Block (Jim McKelvey). Vinoo Ganesh is CEO & Co-Founder; co-founder John McRaven spent 11 years at Palantir. The talk title references Kepler and describes how FDE is practiced there.
organization.status: Active, early-stage company (founded 2025, ~6 employees, based in New York)

technologies.label: Palantir Foundry Ontology System
technologies.summary: The Palantir Foundry Ontology is an operational layer that sits on top of integrated digital assets (datasets, virtual tables, models) and connects them to their real-world counterparts using object types ('nouns') and action types ('verbs'). In the video, the speaker describes it as an accidental discovery at Palantir that emerged from FDE fieldwork: by defining the nouns and verbs of an enterprise, FDEs created a linguistic foundation that locked in customers and enabled subsequent engineers to perform data integrations and sell product. Official Palantir documentation externally confirms the Ontology as the heart of Foundry's architecture, directly matching the talk's 'nouns and verbs' terminology.
technologies.role: Central technology example illustrating how defining enterprise nouns and verbs creates a linguistic foundation that locks in customers and enables downstream product sales. The Ontology is presented as the key strategic outcome of FDE work at Palantir.

technologies.label: Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) Methodology
technologies.summary: Forward Deployed Engineering is a product engineering methodology involving embedding engineers with customers to discover real problems through on-site observation, solving small problems rapidly to build trust, defining enterprise ontology (nouns and verbs), calibrating what to ship into the core product versus discard, and translating field discoveries into platform features that create product leverage. The talk's central thesis, attributed to Palantir CTO Shyam, is that FDE is a product strategy, not a role or go-to-market function. Key principles include: customers describe solutions not problems; whoever defines the problem owns the solution; if solvable in under a day, ship immediately; every hack goes into production so ship everything like it will run for 18 months; and product leverage is the only thing that wins customers. The Phoenix failure (a big data storage system built in isolation that crashed on real data, requiring 14TB of RAM) and the venue.groovy cautionary tale (a temporary script that spread across a 100,000-person customer) illustrate the costs of building without customer embedding and of failing to productize field solutions.
technologies.role: The central methodology that the entire talk is about. The speaker defines FDE as a product strategy, demonstrates its application through multiple field stories (dispatch company, data quality engineer, venue.groovy, Phoenix failure), and argues it is the mechanism for building product leverage that wins customers.

technologies.label: Apache Parquet and Columnar Data Pipeline Migration
technologies.summary: Apache Parquet is a columnar storage data format that was the target of a migration from CSV at a customer site. A data quality engineer named Maria opposed the migration for a year because she needed to visually inspect data by downloading CSVs and double-clicking them on her Windows computer, which Parquet did not support. On-site observation by an FDE revealed this hidden workflow blocker. An overnight-built Parquet viewer tool resolved the issue, Maria approved migration within two days, and pipeline execution time dropped from 17 hours to 2 hours. The story demonstrates that data engineering decisions are constrained by human workflows, and that resolving workflow-level blockers can unlock dramatic technical improvements.
technologies.role: Case study technology demonstrating that data format migration is constrained by human workflows, not just technical specifications. The Parquet migration story is one of two primary field examples used to illustrate the on-site observation principle and the under-a-day shipping rule.

technologies.label: Kepler Ground Truth Platform for AI
technologies.summary: Kepler (kepler.ai) is building 'the ground truth platform for AI'—infrastructure that prevents LLMs from generating unreliable numbers by providing verifiable, traceable outputs, primarily for financial services. The speaker is CEO and Co-Founder and is building the FDE function there, applying the methodology from his seven years at Palantir and subsequent role at Citadel to AI product development. Kepler was founded in early 2026 by ex-Palantir engineers Vinoo Ganesh and John McRaven, and is backed by founders of OpenAI, Facebook AI Research, MotherDuck, dbt, and Outerbounds. The talk title explicitly references Kepler as the current context for FDE practice. It is distinct from Kepler Communications (kepler.space), a Toronto-based satellite company.
technologies.role: Provides the current context for the speaker's application of FDE methodology. The talk is framed as 'How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Kepler,' positioning Kepler as the active environment where the historical lessons from Palantir are being applied to build verifiable AI infrastructure.
